title: Rebound effect

definition.text: The loss of part of the expected savings from a more efficient technology, because people and the economy respond by using more.

facts.text: It is expressed as the share of the expected saving that is lost: if a 5% gain in fuel efficiency cuts fuel use by only 2%, the rebound is 60%.
The 'missing' saving may go into driving faster or further than before.
Most economists agree it exists but disagree about how large and important it is.
It was first described by William Stanley Jevons in his 1865 book The Coal Question, which observed that a more efficient steam engine opened many new uses for coal.
Though studied mostly for energy, the idea applies to any natural resource or input, including labour.
Studies of home heating, cooling and personal transport often find rebounds of 20–50%.
Direct rebounds tend to be higher in low-income households, which have been cutting back on heating because of its cost.

contested_note: Researchers agree the rebound effect exists but disagree about its size and importance for policy.

definition.text: The three ways the economy can take back efficiency savings: the direct, indirect and economy-wide rebound effects.

facts.text: Direct rebound: a good is used more because it has become cheaper to use, as when cheaper driving leads to more driving.
Indirect rebound: the money saved is spent on other goods and services, such as savings from an efficient cooling system spent on a luxury.
Economy-wide rebound: cheaper services lower other prices, open new production possibilities and speed up economic growth.
Indirect effects from household conservation can range from 10% to 200% depending on the scenario.
Even if direct and indirect rebounds add up to less than 100%, faster growth from efficiency can still raise the economy's total resource use.

title: Time rebound effect
article: Rebound effect (conservation)#Rebounds with respect to time

definition.text: Extra resource use that follows when a technology saves people time, which they then spend on more of the service or other activities.

facts.text: Faster transport lowers the real cost of commuting but encourages longer commutes, which raise energy use.
Its scale is almost impossible to measure because people value time subjectively.

definition.text: Measures that keep efficiency gains from being eaten up by extra use, usually by holding the cost of use steady or higher.

facts.text: Wackernagel and Rees suggested that cost savings from efficiency be 'taxed away' and preferably reinvested in restoring natural capital.
Tools include green taxes, cap and trade, higher fuel taxes, or targeting the yearly energy use of a system rather than device efficiency.
Fuel use falls unambiguously if efficiency gains are paired with a measure such as a fuel tax that keeps fuel costs the same or higher.

title: Jevons paradox

definition.text: The observation that making a resource more efficient to use can increase, rather than reduce, total use of that resource.

facts.text: Efficiency lowers the effective cost of using the resource; if demand responds strongly to price, use rises enough to outweigh the saving.
In 1865 William Stanley Jevons saw England's coal use soar after James Watt's more efficient steam engine made coal a cheaper power source for many industries.
It occurs when the rebound effect exceeds 100%, more than wiping out the original efficiency gain.
Its conditions are an efficiency gain, a resulting fall in price to consumers, and demand that rises sharply in response.
Farming productivity gains lowered food prices without raising food demand much, so the paradox did not occur; farm employment instead fell from 40% of Americans in 1900 to under 2% in 2024.
Higher crop yields can make a crop more profitable and lead farmers to convert more land to it, raising land use.
Many environmental economists say efficiency must be paired with policies such as green taxes or cap and trade to cut resource use, while others find limited evidence that the paradox is widespread.

contested_note: Economists debate how often the paradox occurs and how relevant it is to energy-efficiency policy.
